subject: social-studies
title: Living with differences
issue: How can people of different backgrounds live well together?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: Singapore has people of many races, religions and nationalities. Most live in the same housing estates, attend the same schools and eat at the same hawker centres. Living side by side does not, by itself, mean that people understand one another.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which individuals can build understanding between people of different backgrounds.

seeded.text: People can talk to their neighbours and join activities. They can also respect other religions. Singapore has many races living in the same estates.

One way is to take part in each other's festivals. For example, a family can accept a neighbour's invitation to a Hari Raya open house. They eat together and can ask about the fast and the customs. This replaces guesses about the other group with what they have seen for themselves, so there is more understanding. Another way is to respect other religions.

This replaces guesses about the other group with what they have seen for themselves, so there is more understanding. A second way is to speak up against stereotypes. For example, when a classmate jokes that one race is lazy, a student can say that it is not true and not funny. This stops a false idea from spreading in the group, so others learn to judge people by what they do and not by their race.

questions.question: 'Shared experiences do more than government policies to build harmony in a diverse society.' Do you agree? Explain your answer.

seeded.text: I agree because shared experiences are important and people should mix around. Policies are also important in Singapore.

Shared experiences build harmony. For example, in a school CCA, students of different races train together for months and depend on each other to win. They come to trust each other as teammates, so race matters less to them and friendships form across groups.

subject: social-studies
title: Citizens and the needs of society
issue: Who should look after the needs of society?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: A government cannot meet every need in society. Citizens can contribute too, as individuals or through organised groups. Some help directly. Others give feedback so that policies fit people's needs better.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which citizens can contribute to the needs of society.

seeded.text: Citizens can help directly and give feedback so that policies fit people's needs. They can volunteer and donate.

One way is to volunteer with a group that serves people in need. For example, volunteers at a food charity pack and deliver rations to elderly people living alone every week. The government gives financial help but cannot visit every home, so the volunteers meet a need that would be missed. Citizens can also give feedback.

For example, citizens can give their views in a public consultation, such as those run by REACH, before a policy is changed. The government learns how the policy affects ordinary people, so it can adjust the policy to fit their needs better.

questions.question: 'Individuals do more than organised groups to meet the needs of society.' Do you agree? Explain your answer.

subject: social-studies
title: Living in a globalised world
issue: What does globalisation mean for a country and its people?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: Globalisation links countries through trade, travel and technology. Goods, money, people and ideas move across borders faster than before. This brings gains to some and losses to others.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which globalisation can affect workers in a country.

seeded.text: Globalisation links countries through trade, travel and technology. Workers are affected because goods and people move faster. Some gain and some lose.

One way is that workers may lose their jobs. For example, a company can move its factory to a country where wages are lower. The workers in the first country are no longer needed and are retrenched, so they lose their income. Another way is more opportunities.

One way is that workers may lose their jobs. For example, a company can move its factory to a country where wages are lower. The workers in the first country are no longer needed and are retrenched, so they lose their income. A second way is that workers get more job opportunities. For example, when foreign technology firms set up regional offices in Singapore, they hire local staff. Workers have more employers to choose from, so those with the right skills can earn higher pay.

questions.question: 'The economic effects of globalisation matter more to a country than its cultural effects.' Do you agree? Explain your answer.

The economic effects matter. For example, Singapore has few natural resources and earns its living by trading with the world, and foreign companies invest here. This creates jobs and income for its people, so the country can pay for schools and hospitals.

subject: social-studies
title: New arrivals
issue: How do newcomers become part of a society?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: Many countries take in immigrants to work and to settle. Newcomers bring skills and new ideas. They also arrive with different habits and languages, and locals do not always welcome them.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which immigrants can fit into the society they have joined.
questions.model: One way is to learn the common language. For example, a newcomer to Singapore can take English classes so that he can talk with neighbours and colleagues. Once they can speak to each other, small misunderstandings are cleared up, so locals come to see him as a person and not a stranger. A second way is to join in local community life. For example, a new family can help at their residents' committee events or join a neighbourhood sports group. They work beside locals towards the same goal, so trust grows and they are treated as part of the estate.

questions.question: 'Locals have a bigger part to play than newcomers in making integration work.' Do you agree? Explain your answer.
questions.model: Newcomers have a part to play. For example, they can learn English and follow local norms such as queueing and keeping noise down at night. This shows respect for the place they have joined, so locals have less reason to resent them. Locals have a part to play too. For example, they can invite a new neighbour to a block party, or help a new colleague understand how things are done. The newcomer then has a way in, so he does not keep only to people from his own country. Locals have the bigger part, because they are the majority and they set the tone. A newcomer can try hard and still be shut out if locals refuse to mix. When locals are open, even a shy newcomer is drawn in. So I agree: both must act, but the newcomer's effort only works when locals allow it to.

subject: social-studies
title: Paying for healthcare
issue: How should a society share the cost of healthcare?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: People are living longer, and treatment costs more each year. A government has a limited budget and many other needs to pay for. Whatever it spends on healthcare cannot be spent elsewhere.

questions.question: Explain two reasons why a government has to make trade-offs when it decides how much to spend on healthcare.
questions.model: One reason is that the budget is limited. For example, money spent on building a new hospital cannot also be spent on schools or defence. The government has to decide which need comes first, so spending more on healthcare means giving up something else. A second reason is that demand for healthcare keeps growing. For example, Singapore's population is ageing, and older people need more treatment for longer. If the government paid for everything, the cost would rise every year, so it has to choose what to subsidise and what people pay for themselves.

questions.question: 'Keeping people healthy is more the individual's responsibility than the government's.' Do you agree? Explain your answer.
questions.model: Individuals are responsible for their health. For example, a person who exercises, eats sensibly and goes for screening is less likely to develop diabetes or heart disease. Many illnesses come from daily habits, so only the person himself can prevent them. The government is responsible too. For example, it subsidises polyclinics and hospital wards and runs schemes such as MediShield Life. Without these, a serious illness would cost too much for many families, however carefully they lived. The individual's part matters more, judged by how much illness each can prevent. The government can only make treatment affordable after people fall sick, and its help is limited by its budget. A person's habits decide whether he falls sick at all. So I agree: the government must provide a safety net, but staying healthy starts with the individual.

subject: social-studies
title: How governments make decisions
issue: What should a government consider when it makes a decision?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: Every government decision has a price and affects many groups of people. A choice that helps one group may cost another. Some decisions also shape the country for many years after they are made.

questions.question: Explain two factors that a government has to consider when it makes a decision.

seeded.text: A government has to think about money and about what people want. It also has to think about the future. Every decision affects many groups.

One factor is cost. A government has a limited budget, so money spent on one thing cannot be spent on another. For example, MediShield Life covers every citizen and permanent resident for life, even those who are already ill. The government had to find the money to help pay for this cover. So before deciding, it must check that it can afford the policy without cutting other important services. Another factor is the needs of the future.

subject: social-studies
title: Making your views heard
issue: How can citizens make their views heard?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: Citizens often have views on how their country should be run. Some speak to their leaders face to face. Others share their views online, where many people can read them quickly.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which citizens can make their views heard.

seeded.text: Citizens can go online and post their views. They can also speak to their leaders. Everyone has a right to give their opinion.

One way is to take part in a government feedback channel. For example, REACH gathers views on policies through dialogues, surveys and online channels. A citizen can join a dialogue or fill in a survey before a policy is changed. The views reach the officers who make the policy, so the government hears what ordinary people think. Another way is to meet their Member of Parliament.

A second way is to meet their Member of Parliament. For example, MPs hold Meet-the-People Sessions in their constituencies, where residents can raise a problem in person. The MP can write to the ministry concerned or raise the issue in Parliament. So a concern from one resident can be heard by the people who make decisions.

subject: social-studies
title: Disagreeing about the common good
issue: Why do citizens disagree about what is good for society?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: Citizens want what is good for society, but they do not always agree on what that is. A policy that one group welcomes may upset another group. A government has to decide whose views to follow.

questions.question: Explain two reasons why citizens may disagree about what is good for society.

seeded.text: Citizens disagree because they are different. Some people like a policy and some do not. Everyone has their own opinion.

One reason is that a policy affects groups differently. For example, Electronic Road Pricing charges drivers when they use busy roads at peak hours. Bus passengers enjoy smoother roads, but drivers pay more. Each group judges the policy by how it affects them, so they disagree about whether it is good for society. Another reason is that people have different values.

A second reason is that people put different things first. For example, some citizens think the government should spend more now on help for families who need it today. Others think more should be saved for future needs, such as care for an ageing population. Both want a good society but value different things, so they disagree about what is good for it.

questions.question: 'A government should always do what the majority of citizens want.' Do you agree? Explain your answer.

seeded.text: I agree because it is a democracy and the majority should win. But the minority also matters.

A government should listen to the majority. For example, in Our Singapore Conversation in 2012 and 2013, more than 47,000 people shared the future they wanted before plans were made. When a government follows what most people want, its policies fit the needs of most citizens. If it ignored them, it would lose their trust and their votes, so following the majority keeps it accountable to the people it serves.

subject: social-studies
title: Young people and their community
issue: What can young people do for their community?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: Young people are often busy with school, but many still find time to help others. Some join projects in school. Others use skills that older residents may not have.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which young people can improve their community.

seeded.text: Young people can volunteer and help old people. They can also keep their neighbourhood clean. They have a lot of energy.

One way is to volunteer through school projects. For example, students take part in Values in Action projects, such as visiting elderly residents or helping at a food distribution. The students give their time to people who need company or help. So residents who might be left alone are cared for, and the community becomes kinder. Another way is to teach older residents new skills.

For example, young people can teach older residents to use a phone to make payments or book a medical appointment. Many older people were not taught these skills. Once they learn, they can do more on their own and keep in touch with family and services, so they are less left behind.

subject: social-studies
title: Caring for older people
issue: Who should care for older people?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: Singapore has more older people than before, and many are living longer. Older people may need money, healthcare and company. Families, the community and the government all play a part in caring for them.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which the needs of older people can be met.

seeded.text: Older people can be helped by their family and the government. They need money and healthcare. They also need company.

One way is through savings for old age. For example, workers and their employers put part of each month's pay into CPF, and the savings can pay out money every month after retirement. An older person who has stopped working still has an income. So the need for money is met without depending fully on others. Another way is for family members to look after them.

Family members who are close by notice problems early and give company, so the older person is safer and less lonely.

subject: social-studies
title: Why societies become diverse
issue: Why are societies becoming more diverse?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: Many cities today are home to people from many countries. People move for work, for study and for family. Over time, their customs and languages become part of the society they have joined.

questions.question: Explain two reasons why a society becomes more diverse.

seeded.text: Societies become diverse because people move around the world. People come for work and for family. There are many races.

One reason is that people move for work. For example, Singapore needs workers in construction and healthcare, so many workers come from other countries to fill these jobs. They bring their own languages, food and customs. So the society has a wider mix of cultures than before. Another reason is marriage between people of different backgrounds.

One reason is that people move for work. For example, Singapore needs workers in construction and healthcare, so many workers come from other countries to fill these jobs. They bring their own languages, food and customs. So the society has a wider mix of cultures than before. A second reason is marriage across races and nationalities. For example, many Singaporeans marry someone from another country or another race. Their children grow up with two cultures, and the family celebrates the festivals of both sides. So mixed families add new customs to the society from one generation to the next.

questions.question: 'Immigration brings more benefits than challenges to a society.' Do you agree? Explain your answer.

subject: social-studies
title: Living with income differences
issue: How do differences in income affect people?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: In every society, some families earn much more than others. Income affects where people live, what they can buy and the chances their children have. A large gap between rich and poor can also affect how people see one another.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which differences in income can affect the lives of people.

seeded.text: Rich people can buy more things than poor people. Poor people may live in smaller homes. Income affects everyone.

One way is through education. Families with higher incomes can pay for tuition and enrichment classes, while poorer families may not afford them. For example, self-help groups such as CDAC, MENDAKI and SINDA run low-cost tuition because some families cannot pay for it. Without such help, children from poorer homes get less support, so they may do less well in school and have fewer chances later. Another way is through health.

subject: social-studies
title: Respecting religious practices
issue: How can people of different religions live and work well together?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: Schools and workplaces bring together people of many religions. Each religion may have its own prayers, festivals and rules about food. Small acts of respect can help people of different faiths work well side by side.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which people can respect different religious practices at school or at work.

seeded.text: People can respect other religions and not make fun of them. They can learn about other festivals. There are many religions in Singapore.

One way is to make room for practices in daily routines. For example, a workplace can let Muslim staff take time for Friday prayers, and colleagues can avoid fixing meetings at that time. The staff can follow their faith without falling behind at work. So they feel accepted, and people of different faiths work well together. Another way is to learn about other religions.

A second way is to learn the reasons behind the practices of others. For example, a student can ask a Muslim classmate why the classmate fasts during Ramadan, or a class can visit a temple, church or mosque on a learning journey. Words that could divide people can be stopped early, before they spread. So laws set a firm limit that protects harmony.

subject: social-studies
title: Strength in diversity
issue: Does diversity make a society stronger?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: A diverse society has people who speak different languages, follow different religions and keep different customs. Some say this variety is a source of strength. Others worry that differences can lead to tension.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which diversity can strengthen a society.

seeded.text: Diversity is good because there are many races. People can learn new things from each other. There is also more food to eat.

One way is that diversity gives a society links to many parts of the world. For example, many Singaporeans speak a mother tongue such as Mandarin, Malay or Tamil as well as English. They can work and do business with people in China, Malaysia, Indonesia and India more easily. This helps local firms win trade abroad, so the economy grows stronger. Another way is that diversity makes a society more interesting.

subject: social-studies
title: Why misunderstandings happen
issue: Why do people of different backgrounds sometimes misunderstand one another?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: People of different backgrounds may live in the same estate but have little contact with one another. They may also follow customs that others do not know about. Online, people now see more about other groups than ever before.

questions.question: Explain two reasons why misunderstandings can arise between people of different backgrounds.

seeded.text: People have different religions and customs. Some people are racist. Some people do not talk to their neighbours.

A neighbour who does not know the custom may think the family is being noisy and selfish. The neighbour may complain, and the family feels its culture is not respected, so a misunderstanding grows between them. Another reason is that people may be racist.

subject: social-studies
title: Globalisation and local culture
issue: How does globalisation change the culture of a country?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: Today, young people in many countries watch the same shows, wear the same brands and eat at the same fast-food chains. At the same time, many countries work hard to keep their own food, festivals and languages alive.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which globalisation can affect the culture of a country.

One way is that foreign culture spreads into the country and changes what people enjoy. For example, Korean dramas and K-pop are very popular among young people in Singapore, who watch them online and learn Korean words and dances. As they spend more time on foreign shows and music, local and traditional entertainment gets less attention, so the culture of the young becomes more like that of other countries. subject: social-studies
title: Threats across borders
issue: How does globalisation affect the safety of a country?

sources.provenance: An extract to start you thinking. Answer from your own knowledge.
sources.text: Globalisation connects countries through travel, trade and the internet. These links bring many benefits. They also mean that a threat that starts in one country can reach another country quickly.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which globalisation can make a country less safe.

seeded.text: Globalisation brings threats like terrorism, disease and hackers. Countries are connected so it is dangerous.

One way is that diseases can spread quickly from country to country. For example, COVID-19 was first found in China at the end of 2019 and reached Singapore within weeks through travellers. Because so many people fly between countries every day, the virus spread before borders could be closed. Many people fell ill and the country had to go into a circuit breaker in 2020, so people's health and daily lives were put at risk. Another way is that there can be cyber attacks.

A second way is that cyber attacks can come from anywhere in the world. For example, in 2018 hackers stole the personal data of about 1.5 million patients from SingHealth, a public healthcare group. Because hospitals, banks and government services are now online and linked to the global internet, attackers do not need to enter the country to harm it. Private data can be stolen and key services can be disrupted, so the country is less safe.

questions.question: 'Countries protect themselves better by working with other countries than by acting alone.' Do you agree? Explain your answer.

Working with other countries protects a country. For example, since 2004 Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, later joined by Thailand, have patrolled the Straits of Malacca together. The navies share information and cover more sea than one country could alone. Pirates have fewer places to hide, so the busy shipping lanes that Singapore depends on are safer.

subject: social-studies
title: Workers in a changing world
issue: How can individuals cope with the changes that globalisation brings?

sources.text: Globalisation brings new jobs to some countries and takes jobs away from others. Companies move work to wherever it can be done more cheaply or better. Workers today may need to change jobs several times in their lives.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which workers can respond to the changes that globalisation brings.

seeded.text: Workers can study more. They can find a new job. They should not give up.

One way is that workers can keep learning new skills. For example, from 2016 Singaporeans aged 25 and above received SkillsFuture credit to pay for approved courses. title: Technology shrinks the world

seeded.text: Technology like the internet and planes connects the world. Things are faster now. People use phones.

One way is through the internet and communication technology. For example, people can now hold video calls with colleagues in other countries and shop on overseas websites from their phones. Information and orders that once took weeks by post now arrive in seconds. Companies can work with partners anywhere and shoppers can buy from any country, so countries are connected much more quickly. Another way is through planes.

For example, goods are now packed in standard shipping containers that cranes can move straight from ships to lorries, and ports such as Singapore's handle huge numbers of them every day. Loading and unloading is much faster and cheaper than before. Goods can be moved around the world quickly and at low cost, so trade between countries has grown very fast.

questions.question: 'Technology has done more than trade to connect countries.' Do you agree? Explain your answer.

seeded.text: I agree because everyone uses the internet now. Trade is also important to connect countries.

Technology connects countries. For example, through the internet people can video call friends and colleagues overseas, watch foreign shows and follow news from around the world as it happens. Ideas and culture now flow between countries every second. So people in different countries know far more about each other and feel closer than before.

Technology connects countries. For example, through the internet people can video call friends and colleagues overseas, watch foreign shows and follow news from around the world as it happens. Ideas and culture now flow between countries every second. So people in different countries know far more about each other and feel closer than before. Trade also connects countries. For example, Singapore has signed more than 20 free trade agreements, and it buys most of its food and energy from abroad while selling goods and services to the world. Countries that trade depend on each other for their jobs and daily needs. This gives them a strong reason to keep good relations, so trade ties countries together closely.

I disagree, judging by what gives countries a reason to stay linked. Technology is the tool that makes connections faster, but it does not by itself make countries need each other. Trade does, because a country like Singapore cannot feed its people or keep its jobs without it. Much of the technology that connects us, such as container ships and online shopping, was built because people wanted to trade. So trade has done more, and technology has mainly sped it up.
